l: Cell (biology)
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all <color=#3366CC>forms of life</color> or <color=#3366CC>organisms</color>. The term comes from the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> word
cellula meaning 'small room'. A biological cell basically consists of a semipermeable <color=#3366CC>cell membrane</color> enclosing
<color=#3366CC>cytoplasm</color> that contains genetic material. Most cells are only visible under a microscope. Except for highly-<color=#3366CC>differentiated</color>

cell types (examples include <color=#3366CC>red blood cells</color> and <color=#3366CC>gametes</color>) most cells are capable of <color=#3366CC>replication</color>, and <color=#3366CC>protein synthesis</color>.
Some types of cell are motile. Cells <color=#3366CC>emerged on Earth</color> about four billion years ago.
All organisms are grouped into <color=#3366CC>prokaryotes</color> and <color=#3366CC>eukaryotes</color>. Prokaryotes are single-celled and include <color=#3366CC>archaea</color> and
<color=#3366CC>bacteria</color>. Eukaryotes can be single-celled or multicellular. Single-celled eukaryotes include most <color=#3366CC>protists</color>, some species

of <color=#3366CC>fungi</color> (<color=#3366CC>yeasts</color>), and some species of <color=#3366CC>algae</color>. Multicellular eukaryotes include <color=#3366CC>animals</color>, <color=#3366CC>plants</color>, some species of fungi,
and some species of algae. All multicellular organisms are made up of many different types of cell. The <color=#3366CC>diploid cells</color>
that make up the body of an animal or plant are known as <color=#3366CC>somatic cells</color>, which excludes the <color=#3366CC>haploid</color> <color=#3366CC>gametes</color>.
Prokaryotes lack a <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound</color> <color=#3366CC>nucleus</color> and have a nucleoid instead. In eukaryotic cells, the nucleus is enclosed
in the <color=#3366CC>nuclear membrane</color>. Eukaryotic cells contain other <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound organelles</color> such as <color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color>, which
provide energy for cell functions, and <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color>, in plants that create sugars by <color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color>. Other
<color=#3366CC>membrane-less organelles</color> may be <color=#3366CC>proteinaceous</color>, such as the <color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color> present (though different) in both groups. A
unique membrane-bound <color=#3366CC>prokaryotic organelle</color>, the magnetosome has been discovered in magnetotactic bacteria.
Cells were discovered by <color=#3366CC>Robert Hooke</color> in 1665, who named them after their resemblance to cells in a <color=#3366CC>monastery</color>. Cell
theory, developed in 1839 by Matthias Jakob Schleiden and <color=#3366CC>Theodor Schwann</color>, states that all organisms are composed
of one or more cells, that cells are the fundamental unit of structure and function in all organisms, and that all cells
come from pre-existing cells.
Types
Organisms are broadly grouped into <color=#3366CC>eukaryotes</color> and <color=#3366CC>prokaryotes</color>. Eukaryotic cells possess a <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound</color>
<color=#3366CC>nucleus</color>, and <color=#3366CC>prokaryotic cells</color> lack a nucleus but have a nucleoid region. Prokaryotes are single-celled organisms,
whereas eukaryotes can be either single-celled or multicellular. Single-celled eukaryotes include microalgae such as

<color=#3366CC>diatoms</color>, and some <color=#3366CC>yeasts</color>, species of <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>. Multicellular eukaryotes include all <color=#3366CC>animals</color>, and <color=#3366CC>plants</color>, most fungi, and
some species of <color=#3366CC>algae</color>.
Prokaryotes

All <color=#3366CC>prokaryotes</color> are single-celled and include <color=#3366CC>bacteria</color> and <color=#3366CC>archaea</color>, two of the three <color=#3366CC>domains of life</color>. Prokaryotic cells
were likely the first form of <color=#3366CC>life</color> on Earth, characterized by having vital biological processes including <color=#3366CC>cell signaling</color>. They
are simpler and smaller than eukaryotic cells, lack a <color=#3366CC>nucleus</color>, and the other usually present <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound</color>
<color=#3366CC>organelles</color>. <color=#3366CC>Prokaryotic organelles</color> are less complex, and are typically <color=#3366CC>membrane-less</color>. All prokaryotic cells secrete
different substances from their membranes, including exoenzymes, and extracellular polymeric substances.
Most prokaryotes are the smallest of all organisms, ranging from 0.1 to 5.0 m in diameter. The largest bacterium
known, Thiomargarita magnifica, is visible to the naked eye with an average length of 1 cm, but can reach 2 cm.
Bacteria
<color=#3366CC>Bacteria</color> are enclosed in a cell envelope, that protects the interior from the exterior. It generally consists of a <color=#3366CC>plasma</color>
<color=#3366CC>membrane</color> covered by a <color=#3366CC>cell wall</color> which, for some bacteria, is covered by a third layer, a gelatinous <color=#3366CC>bacterial capsule</color>.

The capsule may be <color=#3366CC>polysaccharide</color> as in <color=#3366CC>pneumococci</color>, <color=#3366CC>meningococci</color> or <color=#3366CC>polypeptide</color> as <color=#3366CC>Bacillus anthracis</color> or
hyaluronic acid as in <color=#3366CC>streptococci</color>. <color=#3366CC>Mycoplasma</color> only possess the cell membrane. The cell envelope gives rigidity to the
cell and separates the interior of the cell from its environment, serving as a protective mechanical and chemical filter.
The cell wall consists of <color=#3366CC>peptidoglycan</color> and acts as an additional barrier against exterior forces. The cell wall acts to
protect the cell mechanically and chemically from its environment, and is an additional layer of protection to the cell
membrane. It also prevents the cell from expanding and bursting (cytolysis) from <color=#3366CC>osmotic pressure</color> due to a hypotonic
environment.
The <color=#3366CC>DNA</color> of a bacterium typically consists of a single circular chromosome that is in direct contact with the <color=#3366CC>cytoplasm</color> in
a region called the nucleoid. Some bacteria contain multiple circular or even linear chromosomes. The cytoplasm also
contains <color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color> and various inclusions where transcription takes place alongside translation. Extrachromosomal
DNA as <color=#3366CC>plasmids</color>, are usually circular and encode additional genes, such as those of <color=#3366CC>antibiotic resistance</color>. Linear
bacterial plasmids have been identified in several species of spirochete bacteria, including species of <color=#3366CC>Borrelia</color> which
causes <color=#3366CC>Lyme disease</color>. The prokaryotic cytoskeleton in bacteria is involved in the maintenance of cell shape, <color=#3366CC>polarity</color>
and cytokinesis.
Compartmentalization is a key feature of eukaryotic cells but some species of bacteria, have protein-based
organelle-like microcompartments such as gas vesicles, and carboxysomes, and encapsulin nanocompartments.
Certain membrane-bound <color=#3366CC>prokaryotic organelles</color> have also been discovered. They include the magnetosome of
magnetotactic bacteria, and the anammoxosome of anammox bacteria.
Cell-surface appendages can include <color=#3366CC>flagella</color>, and <color=#3366CC>pili</color>, protein structures that facilitate movement and communication
between cells. The flagellum stretches from the cytoplasm through the cell membrane and extrudes through the cell
wall. <color=#3366CC>Fimbriae</color> are short attachment pili, the other type of pilus is the longer conjugative type. Fimbriae are formed of an
<color=#3366CC>antigenic</color> protein called pilin, and are responsible for the attachment of bacteria to specific receptors on host cells.
Archaea
Archaea are enclosed in a cell envelope consisting of a plasma membrane and a cell wall. An exception to this is the
<color=#3366CC>Thermoplasma</color> that only has the cell membrane. The cell membranes of archaea are unique, consisting of ether-linked
lipids. The prokaryotic cytoskeleton has homologues of eukaryotic <color=#3366CC>actin</color> and tubulin. A unique form of metabolism in the
archaean is methanogenesis. Their cell-surface appendage equivalent of the flagella is the differently structured and
unique archaellum. The DNA is contained in a circular chromosome in direct contact with the cytoplasm, in a region
known as the nucleoid. Ribosomes are also found freely in the cytoplasm, or attached to the cell membrane where
DNA processing takes place.
The archaea are noted for their <color=#3366CC>extremophile</color> species, and many are selectively evolved to thrive in conditions of
extreme heat, cold, acidity, alkalinity, or high salt. There are no known archaean pathogens.
Eukaryotes
A eukaryotic cell can be 2 to 100 times larger in diameter than a typical prokaryotic cell. Eukaryotes can be

single-celled, as in <color=#3366CC>diatoms</color> (microscopic algae), or microfungi such as <color=#3366CC>yeasts</color>, or multicellular, as in <color=#3366CC>animals</color>, <color=#3366CC>plants</color>,
most <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>seaweed</color> (macroalgae). Multicellular organisms are made up of many different types of cell known
overall as <color=#3366CC>somatic cells</color>. Eukaryotes are distinguished by the presence of a membrane-bound <color=#3366CC>nucleus</color> that gives the
eukaryote its name, which means "true nut" or "true kernel", where "nut" means the nucleus.
The nucleus is the largest <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound organelle</color> in the eukaryotic cell. Other organelles present in all eukaryotic

cells are the <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color>, <color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Golgi apparatus</color>, <color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color>, <color=#3366CC>lysosomes</color>, <color=#3366CC>peroxisomes</color>,
endosomes, and vesicles. The contents of the cell are contained within a <color=#3366CC>cell membrane</color>, and together with all the
membranes of the organelles (except the mitochondria) are known as the <color=#3366CC>endomembrane system</color>. All of these
membranes are involved in the secretory and <color=#3366CC>endocytic</color> pathways, modifying, packaging, and transporting proteins and
lipids to and from the <color=#3366CC>trans Golgi network</color>. In <color=#3366CC>mammalian</color> cells, endocytosis includes early, late, and recycling
endosomes.

Some eukaryotes cells including <color=#3366CC>plant cells</color> and <color=#3366CC>fungi</color> have a <color=#3366CC>cell wall</color>. <color=#3366CC>Plastids</color> including <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color> feature mainly in
plant cells. Most cell types include vaults. There are many cell variations among the different eukaryote groups. Many
cells project one or more cellular extensions. And some organelles also project extensions such as stromules from
plastids in plant cells, peroxules from <color=#3366CC>peroxisomes</color>, and matrixules from <color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color>.
Most distinct cell types arise from a single totipotent cell, called a <color=#3366CC>zygote</color>, that <color=#3366CC>differentiates</color> into hundreds of different
cell types during the course of <color=#3366CC>development</color>. Differentiation of cells is driven by different environmental cues (such as
cell–cell interaction) and intrinsic differences (such as those caused by the uneven distribution of <color=#3366CC>molecules</color> during
<color=#3366CC>division</color>).

Eukaryotic cell types include those that make up <color=#3366CC>animals</color>, <color=#3366CC>plants</color>, <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>, <color=#3366CC>algae</color>, and <color=#3366CC>protists</color>. All of which have many
different species and cell differences. A separate grouping of animals and fungi are known as <color=#3366CC>opisthokonts</color>.
Structure
A eukaryotic cell has a <color=#3366CC>cell membrane</color> that surrounds a gel-like <color=#3366CC>cytoplasm</color>. The cytoplasm contains the <color=#3366CC>cytoskeleton</color>,
the cell nucleus, the endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, the Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, <color=#3366CC>peroxisomes</color>, endosomes,
vacuoles and vesicles, and vaults. A eukaryotic cell structure, includes an <color=#3366CC>endomembrane system</color> encompassing the
cell membrane, and all the membranes of the organelles excluding those of the mitochondria. The whole system
cooperates in the modification, packaging, and transport of proteins and lipids.
Cell membrane
The <color=#3366CC>cell membrane</color>, or plasma membrane, is a <color=#3366CC>selectively permeable</color> <color=#3366CC>membrane</color> as an outer boundary of the cell that
encloses the cytoplasm. Underlying, and attached to the cell membrane is the cell cortex, the outermost part of the
actin <color=#3366CC>cytoskeleton</color>. The membrane serves to separate and protect a cell from its surrounding environment and is made

mostly from a <color=#3366CC>lipid bilayer</color> of <color=#3366CC>phospholipids</color>, which are <color=#3366CC>amphiphilic</color> (partly <color=#3366CC>hydrophobic</color> and partly <color=#3366CC>hydrophilic</color>). It has
been best described in the fluid mosaic model.
Embedded within the cell membrane are secretory macromolecular <color=#3366CC>lipoprotein</color> structures called porosomes; and a
number of different channels and pumps involved in <color=#3366CC>actively transporting</color> molecules into and out of the cell. The
membrane is semi-permeable, and selectively permeable, in that it can either let a substance (<color=#3366CC>molecule</color> or <color=#3366CC>ion</color>) pass
through freely, to a limited extent or not at all. Cell surface receptors in the membrane allow cells to detect external
<color=#3366CC>signaling molecules</color> such as <color=#3366CC>hormones</color>.
Cytoplasm
The cell membrane encloses the <color=#3366CC>cytoplasm</color> of the cell that surrounds all of the cell's organelles. It is made up of two
main components, the <color=#3366CC>cytoskeleton</color> made up of protein filaments, and the <color=#3366CC>cytosol</color>. The network of filaments and
microtubules of the cytoskeleton gives shape and support to the cell, and has a part in organising the cell components.
The cytosol is a gel-like substance made up of water, ions, and non-essential biomolecules, and is the main site of
<color=#3366CC>protein synthesis</color>, and degradation. The acidity (pH) of the cytosol is near neutral, and is regulated by transporters in
the cell membrane. Different proteins in the cytoplasm operate optimally at different pHs. The cytosol forms 30 % of the
cell's volume.
Cytoskeleton
The <color=#3366CC>cytoskeleton</color> acts to organize and maintain the cell's shape; anchors organelles in place; helps during <color=#3366CC>endocytosis</color>,
and in the uptake of external materials by a cell.The cytoskeleton is composed of <color=#3366CC>microtubules</color>, intermediate filaments
and <color=#3366CC>microfilaments</color>. There are a great number of proteins associated with them, each controlling a cell's structure by
directing, bundling, and aligning filaments. The outermost part of the cytoskeleton is the cell cortex, or <color=#3366CC>actin</color> cortex, a
thin layer of cross-linked actomyosins. Its thickness varies with cell type and physiology. It directs the transport through
the <color=#3366CC>ER</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Golgi apparatus</color>. The cytoskeleton in the animal cell also plays a part in cytokinesis, in the formation of
the spindle apparatus during <color=#3366CC>cell division</color>, the separation of daughter cells.
Organelles
<color=#3366CC>Organelles</color> are compartments of the cell that are specialized for carrying out one or more functions, analogous to the
<color=#3366CC>organs</color>, such as the heart, and lungs. There are several types of organelles held in the cytoplasm. Most organelles are
membrane-bound, and vary in size and number based on the growth of the host cell. Organelles include the <color=#3366CC>nucleus</color>,

<color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color>, <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color>, <color=#3366CC>Golgi apparatus</color>, <color=#3366CC>lysosomes</color>, <color=#3366CC>peroxisomes</color>, <color=#3366CC>vesicles</color>, and <color=#3366CC>vacuoles</color>.

<color=#3366CC>Membrane-less organelles</color> include the <color=#3366CC>nucleolus</color> in the nucleus, <color=#3366CC>centrosomes</color>, <color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color>, <color=#3366CC>proteasomes</color>, and vaults.
Nucleus
The <color=#3366CC>cell nucleus</color> is the largest organelle in the animal cells and many other eukaryotic cells. It houses the cell's
<color=#3366CC>chromosomes</color>, and is the place where almost all <color=#3366CC>DNA</color> replication and <color=#3366CC>RNA</color> synthesis (transcription) occur. The nucleus
is spherical and separated from the cytoplasm by a double-membraned <color=#3366CC>nuclear envelope</color>. A space between the
membranes is called the perinuclear space. The nuclear envelope isolates and protects a cell's DNA from various
molecules that could accidentally damage its structure or interfere with its processing. During processing, DNA is
<color=#3366CC>transcribed</color>, or copied into a special RNA, called <color=#3366CC>messenger RNA</color> (mRNA). This mRNA is then transported out of the
nucleus, where it is translated into a specific protein molecule. The <color=#3366CC>nucleolus</color> is a specialized biomolecular condensate
within the nucleus where ribosome subunits are assembled. It is one of several types of membrane-less nuclear
bodies. Cells use DNA for their long-term information storage that is <color=#3366CC>encoded</color> in its DNA sequence. RNA is used for

information transport (e.g., <color=#3366CC>mRNA</color>) and <color=#3366CC>enzymatic</color> functions (e.g., <color=#3366CC>ribosomal</color> RNA). <color=#3366CC>Transfer RNA</color> (tRNA) molecules are
used to add amino acids during protein <color=#3366CC>translation</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>DNA</color> of each cell is its genetic material, and is organized in multiple linear molecules, called <color=#3366CC>chromosomes</color>, that
are coiled around <color=#3366CC>histone</color> <color=#3366CC>proteins</color> and housed in the <color=#3366CC>cell nucleus</color>. In humans, the nuclear genome is divided into 46
linear chromosomes, including 22 homologous chromosome pairs and a pair of <color=#3366CC>sex chromosomes</color>. The nucleus is a
<color=#3366CC>membrane-bound organelle</color>.
Endoplasmic reticulum
The <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color> (ER) is a transport network for molecules targeted for certain modifications and specific
destinations, as compared to molecules that float freely in the cytoplasm. The ER has two forms: the <color=#3366CC>rough</color>
<color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color> (RER), which has <color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color> on its surface that secrete proteins into the ER, and the <color=#3366CC>smooth</color>
<color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color> (SER), which lacks ribosomes. The smooth ER plays a role in calcium sequestration and
release, and helps in synthesis of <color=#3366CC>lipid</color>.
Golgi apparatus
The <color=#3366CC>Golgi apparatus</color> processes and packages <color=#3366CC>proteins</color>, and <color=#3366CC>lipids</color>, that are synthesized by the cell. It is organized as a
stack of plate-like structures known as cisternae.
Mitochondria
<color=#3366CC>Mitochondria</color> are self-replicating double membrane-bound organelles that occur in various numbers, shapes, and sizes
in the cytoplasm of the cell. <color=#3366CC>Aerobic respiration</color> in the mitochondria generates the cell's energy by <color=#3366CC>oxidative</color>
<color=#3366CC>phosphorylation</color>, using <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color> to release energy stored in cellular nutrients (typically pertaining to <color=#3366CC>glucose</color>) to generate
<color=#3366CC>adenosine triphosphate</color> (ATP). Mitochondria are descended from bacteria that formed an endosymbiotic relationship
with ancient prokaryotes. Mitochondria multiply by <color=#3366CC>binary fission</color> and have their own DNA contained in multiple small
circular chromosomes. The mitochondrial DNA (<color=#3366CC>mtDNA</color>) is very small compared to nuclear DNA, but it codes for 13
proteins involved in mitochondrial energy production and specific <color=#3366CC>transfer RNAs</color> (tRNAs). Mitochondria also have their
own ribosomes known as mitoribosomes.
Lysosomes
A <color=#3366CC>lysosome</color> is the most acidic compartment in the cell. It contains over 60 different hydrolytic enzymes that need an
acidic environment. They digest excess or worn-out organelles, food particles, and engulfed <color=#3366CC>viruses</color> or <color=#3366CC>bacteria</color>. The
cell could not house these destructive enzymes if they were not contained in a membrane-bound compartment.
Peroxisomes
<color=#3366CC>Peroxisomes</color> are microbodies bounded by a single membrane. A peroxisome has no DNA or ribosomes and the
proteins that it needs are encoded in the nucleus, and selectively imported from the cytosol. Some proteins enter via
the endomembrane reticulum. They have enzymes that rid the cell of toxic <color=#3366CC>peroxides</color>. The enzymatic content of the
peroxisomes varies widely across the species, as it can in an individual organism. The peroxisomes in animal cells are
concentrated in the liver cells and <color=#3366CC>adipocytes</color>.
Vacuoles
<color=#3366CC>Vacuoles</color> sequester waste products. Some cells, most notably Amoeba, have contractile vacuoles, which can pump
water out of the cell if there is too much water.
Ribosomes

A <color=#3366CC>ribosome</color> is a large complex of <color=#3366CC>RNA</color> and <color=#3366CC>protein</color> molecules considered as a <color=#3366CC>membrane-less organelle</color> when freely
found in the cytosol, or as a <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound organelle</color> when located in the <color=#3366CC>rough</color> type of <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color>. They
each consist of two subunits, one larger than the other, and act as an assembly line where <color=#3366CC>messenger RNA</color> from the
nucleus is used to <color=#3366CC>synthesise proteins</color> from amino acids.
Vaults
A vault is a large ribonuclear protein particle, a <color=#3366CC>membrane-less organelle</color>, three times the size of a ribosome but with
only three proteins in contrast to the near hundred in the ribosome. Most human cells have around 10,000 vaults, and
in some types of <color=#3366CC>immune cell</color> there may be up to 100,000. <color=#3366CC>Macrophages</color> have the greatest number of vaults of any
human cell. Vaults are largely overlooked because their functions are purely speculative. They may play a role in
transport from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and may serve as scaffolds for signal transduction proteins. They are
present in normal tissues, and more so in secretory and excretory epithelial cells.
Proteasome
<color=#3366CC>Proteasomes</color> are intricate membrane-less protein complexes responsible for the degradation of regulatory proteins,
and damaged proteins in the cytosol and nucleus. They also function in protein homeostasis, stress response, and in
the control of cell division and signal transduction.
Animal cells
All the cells in an animal body develop from one totipotent <color=#3366CC>diploid cell</color> called a <color=#3366CC>zygote</color>. During the <color=#3366CC>embryonic</color>

<color=#3366CC>development</color> of an <color=#3366CC>animal</color>, the cells <color=#3366CC>differentiate</color> into the specialised <color=#3366CC>tissues</color> and organs of the organism. Different
groups of cells differentiate from the <color=#3366CC>germ layers</color>. The <color=#3366CC>sponge</color> has only one layer. Some other animals known as
diploblasts have two germ layers the ectoderm, and the endoderm. More advanced animals have an extra layer, the
middle mesodermal layer, and are known as triploblastic. Triploblastic animals make up the large <color=#3366CC>clade</color> of <color=#3366CC>Bilateria</color>.
Differentiation results in structural or functional changes to <color=#3366CC>stem cells</color>, and progenitor cells.

The ectoderm gives rise to several different types of <color=#3366CC>epithelial tissues</color> including the <color=#3366CC>skin</color>, and <color=#3366CC>glands</color>, and to the <color=#3366CC>nervous</color>
<color=#3366CC>tissue</color>. Epithelium as mesothelium forms the lining of many organs, and <color=#3366CC>inner cavities</color>. Epithelial cells are joined
together in sheets by way of <color=#3366CC>cell junctions</color>; adherens junctions, and desmosomes bind the cells together, and
hemidesmosomes bind the cells to the <color=#3366CC>basement membrane</color>. All three types are linked to the cell cytoskeleton.
There are an estimated 200 different cell types in the human body. The estimated cell count in a typical adult human
body is around 30 trillion cells, 36 trillion in an adult male, and 28 trillion in a female.
Structure
Like other eukaryotic cells, animal cells are made up of a cell membrane containing a gel like cytoplasm. In this
cytoplasm are a variety of membrane organelles, including all the shared eukaryotic organelles: the cell nucleus, the
endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, the Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, peroxisomes, endosomes, vacuoles and
vesicles, and vaults; as well and <color=#3366CC>centrosomes</color>, which are unique to animal cells.
Centrosome
The <color=#3366CC>centrosome</color> is a membrane-less organelle composed of pericentriolar material and the two <color=#3366CC>centrioles</color>. The
centrosome is the main microtubule organizing center in the animal cell that produces the <color=#3366CC>microtubules</color> key
components of the cytoskeleton. Centrosomes are composed of two <color=#3366CC>centrioles</color> which lie perpendicular to each other in
which each has an organization like a cartwheel, which separate during <color=#3366CC>cell division</color> and help in the formation of the
mitotic spindle. While most other eukaryotes do have centrioles, plants do not and centrosomes are unique to animal
cells.
Animal cell types
Some types of specialized cell are localized to a particular animal group. <color=#3366CC>Vertebrates</color> for example have specialized,
structurally changed cells including <color=#3366CC>muscle cells</color>. The cell membrane of a <color=#3366CC>skeletal muscle cell</color> or of a <color=#3366CC>cardiac muscle</color>
<color=#3366CC>cell</color> is termed the sarcolemma. And the cytoplasm is termed the sarcoplasm. Skeletal muscle cells also become
multinucleated. Populations of animal groups <color=#3366CC>evolve to become distinct species</color>, where sexual reproduction is isolated.
The many <color=#3366CC>species</color> of vertebrates for example have other unique characteristics by way of additional specialized cells.
In some species of electric fish for example modified muscle cells or nerve cells have specialized to become
electerocytes capable of creating and storing electrical energy for future release, as in stunning prey, or use in
electrolocation. These are large flat cells in the <color=#3366CC>electric eel</color>, and <color=#3366CC>electric ray</color> in which thousands are stacked into an
electric organ comparable to a voltaic pile.
Many animal cells are <color=#3366CC>ciliated</color> and most cells except red blood cells have <color=#3366CC>primary cilia</color>. Primary cilia play important roles
in chemosensation and mechanosensation. Each cilium may be "viewed as a sensory cellular <color=#3366CC>antennae</color> that
coordinates a large number of cellular signaling pathways, sometimes coupling the signaling to ciliary motility or
alternatively to cell division and differentiation." The cilia in other cells are motile organelles, and in the respiratory
epithelium play an important role in the movement of mucus. In the reproductive system ciliated epithelium in the
<color=#3366CC>fallopian tubes</color> move the egg from the uterus to the ovary. Motile cilia also known as flagella, drive the sperm cells.
<color=#3366CC>Invertebrate</color> planarians have ciliated excretory flame cells. Other excretory cells also found in planarians are
solenocytes that are long and flagellated.
Plant cells

Plant cells have <color=#3366CC>cell walls</color> composed of <color=#3366CC>cellulose</color>, hemicelluloses, and <color=#3366CC>pectin</color> that are constructed outside the <color=#3366CC>cell</color>
<color=#3366CC>membrane</color>. In <color=#3366CC>sclerenchyma</color> tissue <color=#3366CC>lignin</color> is secreted to form a secondary wall inside the primary cell wall. Cutin is
secreted outside the primary cell wall and into the outer layers of the secondary cell wall of the epidermal cells of
leaves, stems and other above-ground organs to form the plant cuticle. Cell walls perform many essential functions,
they provide shape to form the tissue and organs of the plant, and play an important role in intercellular communication
and plant-microbe interactions. Specialized cell-to-cell communication pathways known as <color=#3366CC>plasmodesmata</color>, occur in
the form of pores in the primary cell wall through which the cell membrane and <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color> of adjacent cells
are continuous.

Organelles in <color=#3366CC>plant cells</color>, include <color=#3366CC>pigment</color>-containing <color=#3366CC>plastids</color>, especially <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color> that contain <color=#3366CC>chlorophyll</color> (also
found in <color=#3366CC>algae</color>), large water-storage <color=#3366CC>vacuoles</color>, and two types of peroxisome. Chloroplasts capture the sun's energy to
make carbohydrates through <color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color>. Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble <color=#3366CC>carotenoid</color> pigments such as orange
carotene and yellow xanthophylls which helps in synthesis and storage. Leucoplasts are non-pigmented plastids and
helps in storage of nutrients. Plastids divide by binary fission. The vacuoles are larger than those in animal cells, and
their membrane transports ions against concentration gradients. One type of peroxisome is in the leaves where it takes
part in photorespiration. The other type is in germinating seeds where it takes part in the conversion of fatty acids into
sugars for the plant's growth. In this peroxisome type the enzymatic content is so different from other groups that it has
an alternative name of glyoxysome. The enzymes are of the glyoxylate cycle.
The plant cytoskeleton is a dynamic structure that has a scaffold of microtubules and microfilaments, but no
intermediate filaments. The microtubule organizing center in plant cells is often sited underneath the cell membrane
where nucleated microtubules often form sheet-like semi-parallel arrays.
<color=#3366CC>Plant hormones</color> are produced by all plant cells. <color=#3366CC>Different hormones</color> act as <color=#3366CC>signaling molecules</color> to control all aspects of
the plant's growth and development including embryogenesis and reproduction, and in pathogen defense.
Algal cells
<color=#3366CC>Algae</color> members are photoautotrophs able to use <color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color> to produce energy. In eukaryotes, photosynthesis is
made possible by the use of <color=#3366CC>plastids</color>, organelles in the cytoplasm known as <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color>.

Photosynthesis is found in both prokaryotic <color=#3366CC>cyanobacteria</color> and multiple <color=#3366CC>clades</color> of <color=#3366CC>eukaryotic algae</color>; <color=#3366CC>red algae</color>, <color=#3366CC>brown</color>
<color=#3366CC>algae</color>, and <color=#3366CC>green algae</color>, which are closely related to <color=#3366CC>land plants</color>.
Alginate is a <color=#3366CC>polysaccharide</color> found in the matrix of the cell walls of <color=#3366CC>brown algae</color>, and has many important uses in the
food industry, and in <color=#3366CC>pharmacology</color>.
Fungal cells
The cells of <color=#3366CC>fungi</color> have in addition to the shared eukaryotic organelles a spitzenkörper in their endomembrane system,
associated with <color=#3366CC>hyphal tip growth</color>. It is a phase-dark body that is composed of an aggregation of membrane-bound
vesicles containing cell wall components, serving as a point of assemblage and release of such components
intermediate between the Golgi and the cell membrane. The spitzenkörper is motile and generates new hyphal tip
growth as it moves forward.
The cell walls of fungi are uniquely made of a chitin-glucan complex. <color=#3366CC>Chloroplasts</color> are not found in fungal cells, their
pigments are instead associated with their cell walls.
Protist cells
The cells of <color=#3366CC>protists</color> may be bounded only by a <color=#3366CC>cell membrane</color>, or may in addition have a <color=#3366CC>cell wall</color>, or may be covered
by a <color=#3366CC>pellicle</color> (in <color=#3366CC>ciliates</color>), a test (in testate amoebae), or a frustule (in <color=#3366CC>diatoms</color>).
Some protists such as <color=#3366CC>amoebae</color> may <color=#3366CC>feed on other organisms</color> and ingest food by phagocytosis. Vacuoles known as
phagosomes in the cytoplasm may be used to draw in and incorporate the captured particles. Other types of protists
are photoautotrophs, providing themselves with energy by photosynthesis. Most single-celled protists are motile, and
generate movement with cilia, flagella, or pseudopodia.
<color=#3366CC>Ciliates</color> have two different sorts of <color=#3366CC>nuclei</color>: a tiny, <color=#3366CC>diploid</color> micronucleus (the "generative nucleus", which carries the
<color=#3366CC>germline</color> of the cell), and a large, <color=#3366CC>ampliploid</color> macronucleus (the "vegetative nucleus", which takes care of general cell
regulation.
Cellular processes
Replication
During <color=#3366CC>cell division</color>, a single cell, the mother cell divides into two daughter cells. This leads to the growth of <color=#3366CC>tissue</color> in
multicellular organisms. <color=#3366CC>Prokaryotic</color> cells divide by <color=#3366CC>binary fission</color>, while <color=#3366CC>eukaryotic</color> cells usually undergo a process of
nuclear division, called <color=#3366CC>mitosis</color>, followed by division of the cell, called cytokinesis. A <color=#3366CC>diploid</color> cell may undergo <color=#3366CC>meiosis</color> to
produce haploid cells, usually four. <color=#3366CC>Haploid</color> cells serve as <color=#3366CC>gametes</color> in multicellular organisms, fusing to form new
diploid cells.
<color=#3366CC>DNA replication</color>, or the process of duplicating a cell's genome, always happens when a cell divides through mitosis or
binary fission. This occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of the <color=#3366CC>cell cycle</color>.
In meiosis, the DNA is replicated only once, while the cell divides twice. DNA replication only occurs before <color=#3366CC>meiosis I</color>.
DNA replication does not occur when the cells divide the second time, in <color=#3366CC>meiosis II</color>. Replication, like all cellular
activities, requires specialized proteins.
Signaling
Cell signaling is the process by which a cell interacts with itself, other cells, and the environment. Typically, the
signaling process involves three components: the first messenger (the <color=#3366CC>ligand</color>), the <color=#3366CC>receptor</color>, and the signal itself. Most
cell signaling is chemical in nature, and can occur with neighboring cells or more distant targets. Signal receptors are
complex proteins or tightly bound multimer of proteins, located in the plasma membrane or within the interior.
Each cell is programmed to respond to specific extracellular signal molecules, and this process is the basis of

<color=#3366CC>development</color>, <color=#3366CC>tissue repair</color>, <color=#3366CC>immunity</color>, and <color=#3366CC>homeostasis</color>. Individual cells are able to manage receptor sensitivity
including turning them off, and receptors can become less sensitive when they are occupied for long durations. Errors
in signaling interactions may cause diseases such as <color=#3366CC>cancer</color>, autoimmunity, and <color=#3366CC>diabetes</color>.
Protein targeting
<color=#3366CC>Protein targeting</color> or protein sorting is the biological mechanism by which <color=#3366CC>proteins</color> are transported to their appropriate
destinations within or outside the cell. Proteins can be targeted to the inner space of an <color=#3366CC>organelle</color>, different intracellular
<color=#3366CC>membranes</color>, the <color=#3366CC>plasma membrane</color>, or to the exterior of the cell via secretion. Information contained in the protein itself
directs this delivery process. Correct sorting is crucial for the cell; errors or dysfunction in sorting have been linked to
multiple diseases.
DNA repair
All cells contain enzyme systems that scan for DNA damage and carry out <color=#3366CC>repair</color>. Diverse repair processes have
evolved in all organisms. Repair is vital to maintain DNA integrity, avoid cell death and errors of replication that could
lead to <color=#3366CC>mutation</color>. Repair processes include nucleotide excision repair, DNA mismatch repair, non-homologous end
joining of double-strand breaks, <color=#3366CC>recombinational repair</color> and light-dependent repair (photoreactivation).
Growth and metabolism
Between successive cell divisions, cells grow through the functioning of cellular metabolism. Cell metabolism is the
process by which individual cells process nutrient molecules. Metabolism has two distinct divisions: <color=#3366CC>catabolism</color>, in
which the cell breaks down complex molecules to produce energy and <color=#3366CC>reducing power</color>, and anabolism, in which the cell
uses energy and reducing power to construct complex molecules and perform other biological functions.
Complex sugars can be broken down into simpler sugar molecules called <color=#3366CC>monosaccharides</color> such as <color=#3366CC>glucose</color>. Once
inside the cell, glucose is broken down to make adenosine triphosphate (<color=#3366CC>ATP</color>), a molecule that possesses readily
available energy, through two different pathways. In plant cells, <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color> create sugars by <color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color>, using the
energy of light to join molecules of water and <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color>.
Protein synthesis
Cells are capable of <color=#3366CC>synthesizing new proteins</color>, which are essential for the modulation and maintenance of cellular
activities. This process involves the formation of new protein molecules from <color=#3366CC>amino acid</color> building blocks based on
information encoded in DNA/RNA. Protein synthesis generally consists of two major steps: <color=#3366CC>transcription</color> and <color=#3366CC>translation</color>.
Transcription is the process where genetic information in DNA is used to produce a complementary RNA strand. This
RNA strand is then processed to give <color=#3366CC>messenger RNA</color> (mRNA), which is free to migrate into the cytoplasm. mRNA
molecules bind to protein-RNA complexes called <color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color> located in the <color=#3366CC>cytosol</color>, where they are translated into
polypeptide sequences. The ribosome mediates the formation of a polypeptide sequence based on the mRNA
sequence. The mRNA sequence directly relates to the polypeptide sequence by binding to <color=#3366CC>transfer RNA</color> (tRNA)
adapter molecules in binding pockets within the ribosome. The new polypeptide chain then <color=#3366CC>folds</color> into a functional
three-dimensional protein molecule.
Motility
Unicellular organisms can move in order to find food or escape predators. Common mechanisms of motion include
<color=#3366CC>flagella</color> and <color=#3366CC>cilia</color>, and the projection of pseudopodia in amoeboid movement. Cells in multicellular organisms can move
during processes such as <color=#3366CC>wound healing</color>, the immune response, and <color=#3366CC>cancer metastasis</color>. In wound healing in animals,
<color=#3366CC>white blood cells</color> move to the wound site to kill the <color=#3366CC>pathogens</color> causing infection. Cell motility involves many receptors,
crosslinking, bundling, binding, adhesion, motor and other proteins. The process is divided into three steps: protrusion
of the leading edge of the cell, adhesion of the leading edge and de-adhesion at the cell body and rear, and
cytoskeletal contraction to pull the cell forward. Each step is driven by physical forces generated by unique segments of
the cytoskeleton.
Navigation, control and communication
In August 2020, scientists described one way cells—in particular cells of a slime mold and mouse pancreatic
cancer-derived cells—are able to navigate efficiently through a body and identify the best routes through complex
mazes: generating gradients after breaking down diffused chemoattractants which enable them to sense upcoming
maze junctions before reaching them, including around corners.
Cell death
<color=#3366CC>Cell death</color> occurs when a cell ceases to carry out its functions, as a result of ageing, or types of cell injury (<color=#3366CC>necrosis</color>).
<color=#3366CC>Programmed cell death</color>, including <color=#3366CC>apoptosis</color>, and <color=#3366CC>autophagy</color> is a natural process of replacing dead cells with new ones.
A separate mode of cellular death is known as a mitotic catastrophe, which occurs during <color=#3366CC>mitosis</color>, following the
improper progression of, or entrance to the <color=#3366CC>cell cycle</color>. This mechanism operates to prevent genomic instability. Other
cell death pathways are described, and include anoikis, pyroptosis, mitoptosis, parthanatos, and necroptosis.
Origins
The origin of cells has to do with the <color=#3366CC>origin of life</color>, which began the history of life on Earth. Small molecules needed for
life may have been carried to Earth on meteorites, created at deep-sea <color=#3366CC>hydrothermal vents</color>, or synthesized by lightning
in a reducing atmosphere. There is little experimental data defining what the first self-replicating forms were. <color=#3366CC>RNA</color> may
have been the earliest self-replicating molecule, as it can both store genetic information and catalyze chemical
reactions. This process required an enzyme to <color=#3366CC>catalyze</color> the RNA reactions, which may have been the early <color=#3366CC>peptides</color>
that formed in hydrothermal vents.
Cells emerged around 4 billion years ago. The first cells were most likely <color=#3366CC>heterotrophs</color>. The early cell membranes were
probably simpler and more permeable than later ones, with only a single fatty acid chain per lipid. Lipids spontaneously
form bilayered <color=#3366CC>vesicles</color> in water, and could have preceded RNA.
<color=#3366CC>Eukaryotic</color> cells were created some 2.2 billion years ago in a process called eukaryogenesis. This is widely agreed to
have involved <color=#3366CC>symbiogenesis</color>, in which an <color=#3366CC>archaean</color> and a <color=#3366CC>bacterium</color> came together to create the first eukaryotic
common ancestor. It evolved into a population of single-celled organisms that included the last eukaryotic common
ancestor, gaining capabilities along the way.
This cell had a new level of complexity, with a nucleus and facultatively aerobic <color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color>. It featured at least one

<color=#3366CC>centriole</color> and <color=#3366CC>cilium</color>, sex (<color=#3366CC>meiosis</color> and <color=#3366CC>syngamy</color>), <color=#3366CC>peroxisomes</color>, and a dormant cyst with a cell wall of <color=#3366CC>chitin</color> and/or
<color=#3366CC>cellulose</color>. The last eukaryotic common ancestor gave rise to the eukaryotes' <color=#3366CC>crown group</color>, containing the ancestors of
<color=#3366CC>animals</color>, <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>, <color=#3366CC>plants</color>, and a diverse range of single-celled organisms. The green plants were created around 1.6 billion
years ago with a second episode of symbiogenesis that added <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color>, derived from <color=#3366CC>cyanobacteria</color>.
Multicellularity
Multicellular behavior is demonstrated by <color=#3366CC>microorganisms</color> that are cloned from a single cell and form visible <color=#3366CC>microbial</color>
<color=#3366CC>colonies</color>. A microbial consortium of two or more species can form a <color=#3366CC>biofilm</color> by the secretion of extracellular polymeric
substances (EPSs). <color=#3366CC>Slime molds</color> consist of different groups of microorganisms grouped together in a multicellular-like
fashion.
The first evidence of multicellularity in an organism comes from <color=#3366CC>cyanobacteria</color>-like organisms that lived between 3 and
3.5 billion years ago. Cyanobacteria are variable in morphology, <color=#3366CC>filamentous forms</color> exhibit functional cell differentiation
such as heterocysts (for nitrogen fixation), akinetes (resting stage cells), and hormogonia (reproductive, motile
filaments). These, together with the intercellular connections they possess, are considered the first signs of
multicellularity.
Multicellularity was made possible by the development of the extracellular matrix (ECM) similar in function to the
bacterial EPS that consists of extracellular polymeric substances. EPS enables microbial cell adhesion, and is believed
to be the first evolutionary step toward multicellular organisms. <color=#3366CC>Basement membranes</color> are a type of specialized
extracellular matrix that surrounds most <color=#3366CC>animal tissues</color>, and are essential in their formation. Extracellular matrix
components of laminin domains, integrated with other proteins such as cadherins have been described in single-celled
motile <color=#3366CC>choanoflagellates</color> that pre-dates the evolutionary emergence of basement membranes, one of the two types of
ECM. The emergence of the basement membrane coincided with the origin of multicellularity. The other type of ECM is
the interstial matrix.
The evolution of multicellularity from unicellular ancestors has been replicated in the laboratory, in evolution
experiments using predation as the selective pressure.
History of research
In 1665, <color=#3366CC>Robert Hooke</color> examined a thin slice of cork under his <color=#3366CC>microscope</color>, and saw a structure of small enclosures. He
wrote "I could exceeding plainly perceive it to be all perforated and porous, much like a honeycomb, but that the pores
of it were not regular". To further support his theory, Matthias Schleiden and <color=#3366CC>Theodor Schwann</color> studied cells of both
animal and plants. What they discovered were significant differences between the two types of cells. This put forth the
idea that cells were fundamental to both plants and animals.
• 1632–1723: <color=#3366CC>Antonie van Leeuwenhoek</color> taught himself to make <color=#3366CC>lenses</color>, constructed basic <color=#3366CC>optical microscopes</color> and
drew protozoa, such as Vorticella from rain water, and <color=#3366CC>bacteria</color> from his own mouth.
• 1665: <color=#3366CC>Robert Hooke</color> discovered cells in <color=#3366CC>cork</color>, then in living plant tissue using an early microscope. In his book
Micrographia he coined the term cell (from <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> cellula, meaning "small room") since they resembled the cells of a
<color=#3366CC>monastery</color>.
• 1839: <color=#3366CC>Theodor Schwann</color> and Matthias Jakob Schleiden elucidated the principle that plants and animals are made
of cells, concluding that cells are a common unit of structure and development, founding the cell theory.
• 1855: <color=#3366CC>Rudolf Virchow</color> stated that new cells come from pre-existing cells by <color=#3366CC>cell division</color> (omnis cellula ex cellula).
• 1931: <color=#3366CC>Ernst Ruska</color> built the first <color=#3366CC>transmission electron microscope</color> at the <color=#3366CC>University of Berlin</color>. By 1935, he had built
an <color=#3366CC>electron microscope</color> with twice the resolution of a light microscope, revealing previously unresolvable
organelles.
• 1981: <color=#3366CC>Lynn Margulis</color> published Symbiosis in Cell Evolution detailing how eukaryotic cells were created by
<color=#3366CC>symbiogenesis</color>.
Territories of the United States
Territories of the United States are subnational geographical and political areas governed as <color=#3366CC>administrative divisions</color>
and <color=#3366CC>dependent territories</color> under the <color=#3366CC>sovereignty</color> of the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>. Although all are subject to the constitutional and

territorial <color=#3366CC>jurisdiction</color> of the <color=#3366CC>U.S. federal government</color>, territories differ from <color=#3366CC>states</color> and <color=#3366CC>Indian reservations</color> in that they are
not inherently sovereign. While states have dual sovereignty and Native American tribes have tribal sovereignty in
relation to the federal government, the self-governing powers of territories ultimately derive from the <color=#3366CC>U.S. Congress</color>, as
per the Territorial Clause in Article IV of the <color=#3366CC>U.S. Constitution</color>. Territories are classified as "organized" or "unorganized"
depending on whether they operate under an organic act, and "incorporated" or "unincorporated" depending on
whether the U.S. Constitution applies fully or partially to them. As areas belonging to, but not integral parts of, the U.S.,

territories are their own distinct <color=#3366CC>nations</color> centered around a collective <color=#3366CC>identity</color> based on their <color=#3366CC>land</color>, <color=#3366CC>history</color>, <color=#3366CC>ethnicity</color>,
<color=#3366CC>culture</color>, and <color=#3366CC>language</color>.
All territories of the U.S. are insular areas. The U.S. has sovereignty over three <color=#3366CC>archipelagos</color> or islands in the

<color=#3366CC>Caribbean Sea</color> and eleven in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>. Five territories (<color=#3366CC>American Samoa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guam</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Northern Mariana</color>
<color=#3366CC>Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>United States Virgin Islands</color>) are permanently inhabited, unincorporated territories; the
other nine, known as the United States Minor Outlying Islands, are small islands, atolls, and reefs with no native (or
permanent) population. Of the 14, only one is classified as an incorporated territory (Palmyra Atoll). Two additional
territories (Bajo Nuevo Bank and Serranilla Bank) are claimed by the U.S. but administered by <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>. Historically,
territories were created to administer newly acquired land, and most eventually attained statehood. The most recent
territory to become a U.S. state was Hawaii on August 21, 1959.
Residents of the U.S. territories cannot vote in United States presidential elections, and they have only non-voting
representation in the U.S. Congress. According to 2012 data, territorial telecommunications and other infrastructure are
generally inferior to that of the continental U.S. and Hawaii. Poverty rates are higher in the territories than in the states,
though poverty thresholds for U.S. territories had not been constructed As of 2009. Three of the territories, namely the
United States Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and Guam, are on the United Nations list of Non-Self-Governing
Territories maintained by the Special Committee on Decolonization.
The territories have embraced a variety of strategies towards their relationship with the United States, with some
advocating for closer integration into the United States, and others opting to remain as independent as possible.
Several territories retain collective or trust ownership of native or indigenous lands, speak their indigenous or native
languages, and retain indigenous cultural practices which might not survive under full incorporation to the United States
framework. Residents of some U.S. territories enjoy a high quality of life, for instance in Guam, which has comparable
health to the United States, and American Samoa, which has a crude death rate of 7.2 per 1,000, compared to the
United States rate of 9.2 per 1,000. Research suggests that indigenous diets and lifestyles play a positive role in
Samoans' health, particularly neonatal mortality rates.
Organized vs. unorganized territories
Definitions
Organized territories are lands under federal sovereignty (but not part of any state or the <color=#3366CC>federal district</color>) that were
given a measure of <color=#3366CC>self-governance</color> by Congress through an organic act subject to the Congress's plenary powers
under the Territorial Clause of the Constitution's Article Four, section 3. The term unorganized historically had two
applications. One application was to a newly acquired region not yet constituted as an organized incorporated territory
(e.g. the <color=#3366CC>Louisiana Purchase</color> prior to the establishment of Orleans Territory and the District of Louisiana). The other
was to a region that was previously part of an organized incorporated territory, but subsequently left "unorganized" after
part of it had been organized and had achieved the requirements for statehood. (E.g., a large portion of Missouri
Territory became unorganized territory for several years after its southeastern section became the state of <color=#3366CC>Missouri</color>.)
Historical practice
The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 created the Kansas and Nebraska Territories, bringing organized government to the
region once again. The creation of Kansas and Nebraska left the Indian Territory as the only unorganized territory in
the Great Plains. In 1858, the western part of the Minnesota Territory became unorganized when it was not included in
the new state of <color=#3366CC>Minnesota</color>; this area was organized in 1861 as part of the Dakota Territory. In 1890, the western half of
the Indian Territory was organized as Oklahoma Territory. The eastern half remained unorganized until 1907, when it
was joined with Oklahoma Territory to form the <color=#3366CC>State of Oklahoma</color>. Additionally, the Department of Alaska was
unorganized from its acquisition in 1867 from <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> until organized as the District of Alaska in 1884; it was organized
as Alaska Territory in 1912. Hawaii was also unorganized from the time of its annexation by the U.S. in 1898 until
organized as Hawaii Territory in 1900.
Regions that have been admitted as states under the <color=#3366CC>United States Constitution</color> in addition to the <color=#3366CC>original thirteen</color> were,
most often, prior to admission, territories or parts of territories of this kind. As the United States grew, the most
populous parts of the organized territory would achieve statehood. Some territories existed only a short time before
becoming states, while others remained territories for decades. The shortest-lived was Alabama Territory at two years,
while New Mexico Territory and Hawaii Territory both lasted more than 50 years.
Of the 50 states, 31 were once part of an organized, incorporated U.S. territory. In addition to the original 13, six

subsequent states never were: <color=#3366CC>Kentucky</color>, <color=#3366CC>Maine</color>, and <color=#3366CC>West Virginia</color> were each separated from an existing state; <color=#3366CC>Texas</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Vermont</color> were both <color=#3366CC>sovereign states</color> (de facto sovereignty for Vermont, as the region was claimed by New York)
when they entered the Union; and <color=#3366CC>California</color> was part of unorganized land ceded to the United States by Mexico in
1848 at the end of the <color=#3366CC>Mexican–American War</color>.
Federal administration of current territories
All of the five major U.S. territories are permanently inhabited and have locally elected territorial legislatures and
executives and some degree of political <color=#3366CC>autonomy</color>. Four of the five are organized, but American Samoa is technically
unorganized. All of the U.S. territories without permanent non-military populations are unorganized.
The Office of Insular Affairs coordinates federal administration of the U.S. territories and freely associated states,
except for Puerto Rico.
On March 3, 1849, the last day of the 30th Congress, a bill was passed to create the U.S. Department of the Interior to
take charge of the internal affairs of United States territory. The Interior Department has a wide range of responsibilities
(which include the regulation of territorial governments, the basic responsibilities for public lands, and other various
duties).
In contrast to similarly named Departments in other countries, the United States Department of the Interior is not
responsible for local government or for civil administration except in the cases of Indian reservations, through the
Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), and island dependencies administered by the Office of Insular Affairs.
Permanently inhabited territories
The U.S. has five permanently inhabited territories: <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color> and the <color=#3366CC>U.S. Virgin Islands</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Sea</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Guam</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Northern Mariana Islands</color> in the <color=#3366CC>North Pacific Ocean</color>, and <color=#3366CC>American Samoa</color> in the South Pacific Ocean.
American Samoa is in the <color=#3366CC>Southern Hemisphere</color>, while the other four are in the <color=#3366CC>Northern Hemisphere</color>. In 2020, their
combined population was about 3.62 million, over 90% of which is accounted for by Puerto Rico alone.
People born in Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands acquire U.S. citizenship
by birth, and foreign nationals residing there may apply for U.S. citizenship by naturalization. People born in American
Samoa acquire U.S. nationality but not U.S. citizenship by birth if they do not have a U.S. citizen parent, as the
American Samoan people have consistently refused birthright citizenship, fearing this would undermine indigenous land
ownership, governance, and culture. U.S. nationals without U.S. citizenship may hold U.S. passports and reside in any
part of the United States without restriction. However, to become U.S. citizens they must apply for naturalization, like
foreigners, and may only do so while residing in parts of the United States other than American Samoa. Foreign
nationals residing in American Samoa cannot apply for U.S. citizenship or U.S. nationality at all.
Each territory is self-governing with three branches of government, including a locally elected governor and a territorial
legislature. Each territory elects a non-voting member (a non-voting resident commissioner in the case of Puerto Rico)
to the <color=#3366CC>U.S. House of Representatives</color>. Although they cannot vote on the passage of legislation, they can introduce
legislation, have floor privileges to address the house, be members of and vote in committees, are assigned offices and
staff funding, and may nominate constituents from their territories to the <color=#3366CC>Army</color>, Naval, Air Force and Merchant Marine
academies.
As of the 119th Congress, the territories are represented by Uifa’atali Aumua Amata Radewagen (R) of American
Samoa, James Moylan (R) of Guam, Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R) of Northern Mariana Islands, Pablo Hernández Rivera
(D-PPD) of Puerto Rico and Stacey Plaskett (D) of U.S. Virgin Islands. The <color=#3366CC>District of Columbia</color>'s delegate is Eleanor
Holmes Norton (D); like the district, the territories have no vote in Congress and no representation in the <color=#3366CC>Senate</color>.
Additionally, the <color=#3366CC>Cherokee Nation</color> has delegate-elect Kimberly Teehee, who has not been seated by Congress.
Every four years, U.S. political parties nominate presidential candidates at conventions which include delegates from
the territories. U.S. citizens living in the territories can vote for presidential candidates in these primary elections but not
in the general election.
The territorial capitals are Pago Pago (American Samoa), Hagåtña (Guam), <color=#3366CC>Saipan</color> (Northern Mariana Islands), <color=#3366CC>San</color>
<color=#3366CC>Juan</color> (Puerto Rico) and Charlotte Amalie (U.S. Virgin Islands). Their governors are Pula Nikolao Pula (American
Samoa), Lou Leon Guerrero (Guam), David M. Apatang (Northern Mariana Islands), Jenniffer González-Colón (Puerto
Rico) and Albert Bryan Jr. (U.S. Virgin Islands).
Among the inhabited territories, Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is available only in the Northern Mariana Islands;
however, in 2019 a U.S. judge ruled that the federal government's denial of SSI benefits to residents of Puerto Rico is
unconstitutional. This ruling was later overturned by the <color=#3366CC>U.S. Supreme Court</color>, allowing for the exclusion of territories
from such programs. In the decision, the court explained that the exemption of island residents from most federal
income taxes provides a "rational basis" for their exclusion from eligibility for SSI payments.
American Samoa is the only U.S. territory with its own immigration system (a system separate from the United States
immigration system). American Samoa also has a communal land system in which 90% of the land is communally
owned; ownership is based on the Samoan system of governance, in which a political entity called a matai own land
communally and administers it on behalf of the polity or nu'u.
History
• American Samoa: territory since 1900; after the end of the <color=#3366CC>Second Samoan Civil War</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Samoan Islands</color> were
divided into two regions. The U.S. took control of the eastern half of the islands. In 1900, the Treaty of Cession of
Tutuila took effect. The Manua Islands became part of American Samoa in 1904, and Swains Island became part
of American Samoa in 1925. Congress ratified American Samoa's treaties in 1929. For 51 years, the U.S. Navy
controlled the territory. American Samoa is locally self-governing under a constitution last revised in 1967. The first
elected governor of American Samoa was in 1977, and the first non-voting member of Congress was in 1981. By
<color=#3366CC>jus soli</color>, people born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals, but not U.S. citizens. American Samoa is technically
unorganized, and its main island is Tutuila.
• Guam: territory since 1899, acquired at the end of the <color=#3366CC>Spanish–American War</color>. Guam is the home of Naval Base
Guam and Andersen Air Force Base. It was organized under the Guam Organic Act of 1950, which granted U.S.
citizenship to Guamanians and gave Guam a local government. In 1968, the act was amended to permit the
election of a governor.
• Northern Mariana Islands: A commonwealth since 1986, the Northern Mariana Islands together with Guam were
part of the <color=#3366CC>Spanish Empire</color> until 1899 when the Northern Marianas were sold to the <color=#3366CC>German Empire</color> after the
Spanish–American War. Beginning in 1919, they were administered by Japan as a <color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color> mandate
until the islands were captured by the United States in the Battle of Saipan and Battle of Tinian (June–August
1944) and the surrender of Aguiguan (September 1945) during <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>. They became part of the <color=#3366CC>United</color>
<color=#3366CC>Nations Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands</color> (TTPI) in 1947, administered by the United States as U.N. trustee. The
other constituents of the TTPI were <color=#3366CC>Palau</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Federated States of Micronesia</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Marshall Islands</color>. Following
failed efforts in the 1950s and 1960s to reunify Guam and the Northern Marianas, a covenant to establish the
Northern Mariana Islands as a commonwealth in political union with the United States was negotiated by
representatives of both political bodies; it was approved by Northern Mariana Islands voters in 1975, and came into
force on March 24, 1976. In accordance with the covenant, the Northern Mariana Islands constitution partially took
effect on January 9, 1978, and became fully effective on November 4, 1986. In 1986, the Northern Mariana Islands
formally left U.N. trusteeship. The abbreviations "CNMI" and "NMI" are both used in the commonwealth. Most
residents in the Northern Mariana Islands live on <color=#3366CC>Saipan</color>, the main island.
• Puerto Rico: unincorporated territory since 1899; Puerto Rico was acquired at the end of the Spanish–American
War, and has been a U.S. commonwealth since 1952. Since 1917, Puerto Ricans have been granted U.S.
citizenship. Puerto Rico was organized under the Puerto Rico Federal Relations Act of 1950 (Public Law 600). In
November 2008, a U.S. District Court judge ruled that a series of Congressional actions have had the cumulative
effect of changing Puerto Rico's status from unincorporated to incorporated. The issue is proceeding through the
courts, however, and the U.S. government still refers to Puerto Rico as unincorporated. A Puerto Rican attorney
has called the island "semi-sovereign". Puerto Rico has a statehood movement, whose goal is to make the territory
the 51st state. See also Political status of Puerto Rico.
• U.S. Virgin Islands: purchased by the U.S. from <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color> in 1917 and organized under the Revised Organic Act of
the Virgin Islands in 1954. U.S. citizenship was granted in 1927. The main islands are Saint Thomas, Saint John
and Saint Croix.
Statistics
Except for Guam, the inhabited territories lost population in 2020. Although the territories have higher poverty rates
than the mainland U.S., they have high <color=#3366CC>Human Development Indexes</color>. Four of the five territories have another official
language, in addition to English.
The territories do not have administrative <color=#3366CC>counties</color>. The U.S. Census Bureau counts Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities, the
U.S. Virgin Islands' three main islands, all of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands' four municipalities, and American
Samoa's three districts and two atolls as county equivalents. The Census Bureau also counts each of the U.S. Minor
Outlying Islands as county equivalents.
For statistical purposes, the U.S. Census Bureau has a defined area called the "Island Areas" which consists of
American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (every major territory except Puerto
Rico). The U.S. Census Bureau often treats Puerto Rico as its own entity or groups it with the states and D.C. (for
example, Puerto Rico has a QuickFacts page just like the states and D.C.) Puerto Rico data is collected annually in
American Community Survey estimates (just like the states), but data for the other territories is collected only once
every ten years.
